strengths: The paper identifies important deficiencies in nearest-neighbor fidelity and coverage metrics and proposes two simple, computationally practical modifications: clipping per-sample contributions and, for fidelity, clipping neighborhood radii.

The coverage calibration is accompanied by a clear derivation under an i.i.d., continuous-distribution contamination model, and the implementation reduces memory requirements relative to pairwise-distance implementations.

The empirical study is broad in dataset and baseline coverage, including controlled CIFAR-10 and Gaussian tests, 42 generated datasets across four image benchmarks, sensitivity analysis, implementation checks, and comparison with a recent sanity-check benchmark.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful failure-case illustrations and transparent reporting of computational requirements and limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim of absolute interpretability is substantially overstated. A score of x corresponds to x good samples only under the narrow construction in which good samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and bad samples lie outside every reference neighborhood. General generator errors—partial distortions, density shifts, mode imbalance, near-distribution artifacts, or mixtures of heterogeneous quality—do not admit this interpretation. Consequently, conclusions such as a model being equivalent to 40% good and 60% bad samples are not justified by the theory.

The strongest empirical result, linear degradation under progressively inserted bad samples, largely follows by construction: Clipped Density averages capped per-sample scores, while Clipped Coverage explicitly applies a transform derived to linearize this exact contamination experiment. This does not establish calibration for other practically relevant deficiencies.

Global median radius clipping can suppress legitimate low-density modes and tail regions rather than merely removing outliers. Normalizing the aggregate score on real data does not correct the resulting subgroup-dependent distortion, and the paper provides no analysis of performance across rare versus common modes or imbalanced classes.

The real-model experiments provide rankings and scatter plots but no external validation that those rankings reflect perceptual fidelity, semantic coverage, expert judgment, downstream utility, or known controlled deficiencies. Thus they demonstrate applicability, not correctness of the proposed scores or their absolute semantics.

The paper's own benchmark comparison shows that both proposed metrics fail numerous purpose, data, and bounds checks. Some failures are dismissed by disputing thresholds or criteria, but the broader discrepancy between these results and the claim of a trustworthy general evaluation framework remains unresolved.

The theoretical coverage calibration assumes continuous distributions, effectively tie-free distances, and a particular i.i.d. relationship between real and good synthetic samples. Robustness to finite-sample variation, discrete data, duplicate or memorized samples, unequal sample sizes, and violations of these assumptions is insufficiently characterized.

Evaluation is restricted primarily to image embeddings from a single representation model, DINOv2. Since nearest-neighbor geometry and the proposed radius clipping are highly representation-dependent, the lack of an embedding-model sensitivity study limits the generality of the conclusions.

Overall, the underlying metric modifications are plausible and the evaluation is substantial, but the evidence does not support the paper's defining claim of meaningful absolute scores. Correcting that claim and validating the metrics against independent notions of quality would require major additional work rather than a minor revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: separately evaluating fidelity and coverage while seeking robustness and interpretable scores.

The proposed metrics are simple, computationally feasible modifications of established nearest-neighbor metrics. Clipping per-sample contributions directly prevents a few high-scoring samples from compensating for many obvious failures.
The derivation of the expected unnormalized Clipped Coverage under identical continuous distributions is useful, and the appendix provides a reasonably clear proof and implementation discussion.

The empirical study includes numerous baselines, synthetic stress tests, four real image datasets, many generator families, an implementation-validation table, hyperparameter analysis, and additional benchmark experiments.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful visualizations of known failure modes of Density and Recall.
weaknesses: The central claim of absolute interpretability is not established. The calibration only supports a highly specific contamination model in which 'good' samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and 'bad' samples lie outside every reference ball. A score of 0.4 for an arbitrary generator therefore cannot generally be interpreted as '40% good samples and 60% bad samples,' as the paper repeatedly does.

Clipped Density's global median radius threshold can systematically discard legitimate low-density regions, rare modes, and distribution tails. This changes the target distribution rather than merely making its estimation robust. The paper neither characterizes this bias theoretically nor evaluates performance on realistic imbalanced or long-tailed data.

The desired linear degradation test is partly built into the metrics and is too narrow to validate metric quality. For Clipped Density, averaging capped per-sample scores makes linear degradation under replacement by trivially distant noise nearly tautological; for Clipped Coverage, the transformation is explicitly constructed to produce that curve under the assumed model.

The experiments use Gaussian-noise images as 'bad' samples, an unrealistically easy form of distribution shift. There is little evaluation with subtle artifacts, near-distribution errors, class imbalance, rare-mode loss, adversarial samples, or mixtures in which the good component differs from the reference distribution.

The paper's own external benchmark reveals many failures, including sample-size, bounds, and geometric sanity checks. Several unfavorable outcomes are dismissed as overly strict or based on an allegedly inappropriate criterion, but no independent validation is supplied to justify redefining these criteria.

The real-generator evaluation lacks external ground truth: there is no human study, downstream-task validation, controlled quality ranking, or correlation with established assessments. Observing that diffusion models often rank above GANs is insufficient evidence that the new scores measure perceptual fidelity or coverage correctly.

The reported dependence of scores on training-dataset size is a serious confound, not evidence for meaningful absolute interpretation. Scores cannot serve as universal quality thresholds if otherwise comparable model quality changes substantially with reference-set size or density.
Important design choices remain heuristic, especially clipping radii at the median and using k=5. The sensitivity study covers only one dataset/model pair and still shows systematic variation with k.

Novelty is limited: the main ingredients are clipping nearest-neighbor counts, globally clipping radii, and applying a monotone calibration. The paper does not provide a broader consistency result or formal robustness guarantee showing that these choices estimate well-defined population-level fidelity and coverage quantities.

Reproducibility is incomplete: although parameters, compute estimates, and data sources are described, the manuscript does not provide an accessible implementation of the proposed metrics or complete experiment code. Reproducing all reported experiments is also estimated to require roughly 120 GPU-hours.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: separating fidelity from coverage while making generative-model evaluation more robust and interpretable.

The proposed metrics are simple, computationally practical modifications of established nearest-neighbor metrics. Clipping per-sample contributions directly addresses a clear failure mode, while the coverage calibration is supported by a useful analytical derivation.

The evaluation is broad and unusually thorough, covering controlled contamination, mode dropping, distribution shifts, image distortions, toy distributions, four major image datasets, many generator families, and a recent metric benchmark.
Comparisons include numerous relevant baselines, implementation-equivalence checks, ablations of the Density modifications, sensitivity analysis for k, and detailed computational requirements.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, and the empirical results consistently demonstrate improved behavior in the authors' principal stress tests.
weaknesses: The central absolute-interpretability claim is stronger than the theory supports. A score of x is equivalent to x good samples only under a specific contamination model in which good samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and bad samples contribute exactly zero; it should not generally be interpreted as the actual percentage of acceptable generated samples. The chest-X-ray discussion particularly overstates this interpretation.

For Clipped Coverage, the derivation calibrates the expected unnormalized statistic and then applies a nonlinear inverse to an observed statistic. It does not establish that the expectation of the final transformed score equals 1-x at finite sample sizes, since generally E[g(S)] is not g(E[S]).

Clipping every fidelity-ball radius at the global median is somewhat heuristic and may penalize legitimate low-density regions or minority modes. Experiments with strongly imbalanced multimodal distributions are needed to show that robustness is not obtained at the expense of systematic underweighting of rare but valid samples.

The recent sanity-check benchmark gives a mixed picture: both proposed metrics still fail many purpose and bounds tests, especially Clipped Coverage. The paper discusses only a few disputed failures and therefore does not fully reconcile these results with its broad claims of trustworthy evaluation.

The real-model experiments provide plausible rankings but little external validation that the resulting absolute values correspond to human judgments, downstream utility, or clinically meaningful quality. Dependence on the chosen DINOv2 representation also remains largely unexplored.

strengths: The paper addresses an important weakness of generative-model evaluation: nearest-neighbor fidelity and coverage metrics can be dominated by outliers and yield poorly interpretable values.
Clipping per-sample contributions is intuitive, computationally practical, and supported by clear failure examples. The separate treatment of fidelity and coverage is also well motivated.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering controlled Gaussian experiments, CIFAR-10 perturbations, multiple image datasets and model families, human judgments, rare modes, distortions, time series, and music.
The paper compares against numerous relevant baselines, examines sensitivity to k and sample size, reports computational requirements, and checks reimplementations against original code.
The beta-binomial analysis for unnormalized Clipped Coverage provides useful theoretical grounding for its finite-sample calibration.
weaknesses: The central claim of meaningful absolute interpretation is substantially overstated. Calibration is established only for a specific mixture in which good samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and bad samples lie outside every real k-NN ball. A score of 0.4 for an arbitrary generator therefore does not generally imply quality equivalent to 40% good and 60% bad samples in a task-independent sense.

There appears to be an inconsistency in the definition of the Clipped Coverage calibration. After reversing the decreasing expected-score sequence into ascending order, an ascending insertion index corresponds to the number of good samples, suggesting g(s)=i(s)/M rather than 1-i(s)/M. The empirical plots evidently use the intended direction, but the stated central equation is not reproducible as written.

Lemma 1 silently relies on continuity and absence of distance ties, although its statement only assumes identical real and synthetic distributions. The benchmark's failure on discrete data illustrates that this omitted condition is practically consequential.

Clipping every real-ball radius at the global median can label valid samples from legitimate low-density or minority modes as low-fidelity. The paper tests missing rare modes for coverage but does not test fidelity when the generator correctly produces a rare real subpopulation; this is particularly concerning given the high-stakes and medical-use motivation.

The human evaluation reports correlations only for the proposed metrics, without comparable correlations for the competing metrics. It therefore shows some external validity but does not establish the claimed superiority, and neither proposed metric correlates significantly with human judgments on FFHQ.

On the cited independent benchmark, the proposed metrics still fail many desiderata, including varying sample size, discrete data, hypersphere structure, and several bounds tests. Reclassifying a small subset of failures does not support the broad claim that the new metrics overcome the limitations of existing methods.

Cross-dataset conclusions—especially attributing score ranges to training-set size and interpreting CIFAR-10/FFHQ scores as evidence that 60% of samples are effectively bad—are speculative because embedding geometry, reference-sample composition, dimensionality, and dataset complexity all change simultaneously.

The modifications are relatively simple heuristics, and the lack of an asymptotic characterization leaves unclear what population quantities the metrics estimate. Overall, the extensive empirical work is promising, but the evidence does not yet justify the strongest interpretability and trustworthiness claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: separating fidelity from coverage while improving robustness and interpretability of generative-model evaluation.
The proposed metrics are simple, computationally feasible modifications of Density and Coverage, and the motivation for clipping sample contributions and nearest-neighbor radii is intuitive.

The empirical study is unusually extensive, including controlled contamination tests, mode dropping, distribution shifts, hyperparameter and sample-size analyses, multiple image datasets, music and time-series examples, implementation checks, and comparisons with many baselines.
The appendices provide useful implementation details, computational costs, component-wise analyses, and a derivation of the expected unnormalized Clipped Coverage under an idealized setting.
weaknesses: The central claim of generally meaningful absolute scores is not justified. Calibration is derived only for a specific contamination model in which good samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and bad samples fall outside every real nearest-neighbor ball. Arbitrary generative errors—near-distribution artifacts, density distortions, partial mode collapse, memorization, or semantic errors—need not admit the claimed interpretation as a percentage of good samples.

The definition of an 'equivalent proportion of good samples' is largely induced by applying an inverse calibration curve to a scalar statistic. Without independent validation that equal scores correspond to equal practical quality across qualitatively different failure modes, this is not a substantive absolute interpretation. The paper nevertheless uses scores such as 0.06 to make strong claims about percentages of good medical images and fitness for purpose.

Lemma 1 is stated for identical distributions without the continuity and no-ties assumptions used in its proof. The probability-integral-transform step is not valid as written for arbitrary discrete distributions, consistent with failures reported on discrete benchmark cases.

The experiments favor very easy, far-out-of-distribution 'bad' samples such as Gaussian-noise images. These tests largely encode the assumptions used to design the metrics and provide weak evidence for robustness to realistic artifacts that remain close to the data manifold.

Validation on real generative models is inconclusive because ground-truth fidelity and coverage are unknown. Human correlations reuse a limited existing evaluation, involve few models per dataset, and completely fail on FFHQ; no uncertainty analysis establishes that the proposed metrics outperform competing metrics in agreement with human judgments.

The metric can saturate at one for models concentrated in high-density subsets, discarding fidelity distinctions exactly when truncation or guidance changes the target distribution. The appendix shows unclipped values substantially above one, exposing tension between the bounded definition and the behavior the authors sometimes regard as informative.

The proposed changes—clipping counts, clipping radii at the median, normalizing by a real-data estimate, and numerically remapping coverage—are technically modest. Their novelty would be adequate only if the broad interpretability claims were convincingly established.

The recent benchmark results remain mixed, with many failed desiderata. Several failures are dismissed by relaxing thresholds or reinterpreting benchmark criteria rather than demonstrating robustness under the original evaluation protocol.

Claims concerning deployment and safety in medical imaging are substantially stronger than the evidence and lack clinical validation or an explicit discussion of the risks of treating embedding-space scores as safety thresholds. Overall, the extensive evaluation is valuable, but the unsupported central interpretation prevents the work from being competitive at the stated venue.

strengths: Introduces a clear and practically relevant pair of fidelity/coverage metrics with simple, motivated modifications: clipping per-sample contributions, controlling nearest-neighbor radii for fidelity, and calibrating coverage.
Provides a sound analytical derivation for expected Clipped Coverage under the stated i.i.d. continuous-distribution setting, together with useful implementation and computational-complexity details.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering controlled sanity checks, numerous competing metrics, four image benchmarks and many generators, human judgments, sample-size and hyperparameter sensitivity, distortions, failure modes, time series, and music.

The proposed metrics consistently behave well on the authors' principal contamination, mode-dropping, and outlier tests. The analysis of how a handful of atypical CIFAR-10 samples inflate Density is especially convincing.

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and candid about several limitations. Reimplementation checks against original baseline implementations and detailed runtime reporting strengthen reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claim of absolute interpretability is substantially stronger than the evidence. A score of x is calibrated to x only under a specific contamination model in which good samples are i.i.d. from the reference distribution and bad samples fall outside every real neighborhood. Arbitrary artifacts, near-distribution errors, density shifts, and mode distortions need not map to an equivalent proportion of good samples. Consequently, interpretations such as “0.4 means 40% good and 60% bad” are potentially misleading.

Lemma 1 implicitly requires continuity and effectively tie-free distances, although its statement claims the result whenever the distributions are identical. Discrete or highly duplicated data violate the probability-integral-transform step; fittingly, both proposed metrics fail the benchmark's discrete-versus-continuous tests.

Clipping all fidelity radii at the global median may treat legitimate low-density regions or rare modes as low-fidelity. The evaluation does not adequately isolate this issue using strongly heterogeneous but valid reference distributions, so robustness to outliers may come at an insufficiently characterized bias against rare samples.

The recent external sanity-check benchmark gives a mixed rather than decisive result: the proposed metrics still fail many purpose, sample-size, geometry, and bounds tests. Reclassifying or disputing several benchmark failures is sometimes reasonable, but it weakens the broad claim that the deficiencies of existing metrics have been resolved.

Real-model validation is less conclusive than the controlled tests. Human correlations involve relatively few models, fail entirely on FFHQ, and are not compared directly against all baselines' correlations. The observed model rankings therefore do not independently establish that the proposed metrics measure the intended concepts better.

There are presentation and numerical inconsistencies in the rare-mode experiment: the stated fractions of truck samples and fractions of the complete dataset do not agree with the reported sample counts and plot axes. This does not invalidate the central contribution but reduces confidence in that particular sensitivity claim.
